title: Creating a pocket universe: “Shippers,” fan fiction, andthe X‐Filesonline
finding: Ethnography of the online X-Files 'Shipper' community (qualitative, no sample size in abstract): the mostly female shippers hypothesised an unfolding romance between Mulder and Scully and wanted the characters' equal professional partnership to be the basis of that romance, resisting male-oriented conventions.
why_for_us: Fans of a working duo invest in the romance precisely because the two are equals at work; Kuba and Zosia should be shown as competent peers whose bond grows out of solving the case together, not as a rescue fantasy.

title: Resisting the romance: ‘Shipping’ and the discourse of genre uniqueness in Doctor Who fandom
finding: Grounded analysis of a LiveJournal Doctor Who community (qualitative): when romance was added to a genre show, fans built their identity by othering both 'romance-hating anoraks' and 'romance-obsessed shippers'; genre hybridity became a point of struggle over what the show is.
why_for_us: Adding romance to a procedural can split the audience: part of a notary audience came for the legal thriller and may resent a love plot, so the romance must stay secondary and never replace the case.

title: Swan Queen, shipping, and boundary regulation in fandom
finding: Analysis of Tumblr posts and comments (qualitative): shipping a pairing of two female Once Upon a Time characters led to intense infighting; shipper communities regulate inclusion and exclusion through boundaries performed on digital forums.
why_for_us: Comment sections under a couple storyline can become contentious; plan moderation for Facebook/YouTube comments and do not bait 'ship wars' in a B2B brand channel.

title: Il fandom delle serie tv e l’esperienza dello shipping
finding: Digital ethnography plus qualitative interviews with shippers of The 100 (essay-style study, Italian): shipping is declaring affinity for a pairing and wishing it to become romantic; fans discuss ships on social networks, create derivative stories and quarrel to defend their pairing ('ship wars').
why_for_us: A will-they/won't-they pair gives viewers something to root for and discuss between 60-90 s episodes; leave small, open questions about Kuba and Zosia for the comments.

title: Shippers and Kinnies: Re-conceptualizing Parasocial Relationships with Fictional Characters in Contemporary Fandom
venue: International Conference on the Foundations of Digital Games (FDG)
finding: Conceptual paper with a taxonomy (no empirical sample in abstract): introduces fan terms such as 'shippers' and offers a taxonomy of character-appeal factors that lead fans into parasocial relationships with fictional characters.
why_for_us: Useful vocabulary for briefing writers: viewers attach to the pair through specific character appeal, so each apprentice needs a distinct, likeable trait, not just 'being in love'.

title: Chinese Fandom of Thai Boys’ Love Dramas: Shipping the Queer Romance and Fan Service Practices
finding: In-depth interviews with 30 Chinese viewers: Thai BL series encourage on- and off-screen intimacy between actors; fans' shipping and 'fan service' create a hyperreal experience blurring fiction and reality, which fans co-construct to meet emotional and social needs.
why_for_us: Industry can deliberately fuel shipping with off-screen content (e.g., actor behind-the-scenes clips), but for a notary SaaS brand blurring the actors' real lives with the romance carries reputational risk; keep it in-story.

title: Factors Influencing Emotion Sharing Intention Among Couple-fans of Movie and TV Drama on Social Media: The Case of China
venue: The Institute of Management and Economy Research
finding: Online survey of 504 Weibo 'CP' (couple-pairing) fans, PLS-SEM: per authors, intrinsic motivation (self-determination) and interpersonal relationships significantly predicted intention to share couple-related content, while the social-media environment played a smaller role.
why_for_us: Sharing of couple content is driven by viewers' own emotional need, not by platform nudges; a satisfying couple beat is a better share trigger than a 'share this' call to action.

title: Watching the romance together: the affective audiences in A Dream of Splendor
finding: Content analysis of bullet-comments on the most-viewed Chinese drama of 2019-2022 (debated by about half a million fans per author): co-viewing comments let audiences playfully negotiate gender and sexuality around the romance, shifting attention away from the original drama.
why_for_us: Romance generates comment activity, but the debate can drift to gender politics; for a professional audience, keep romantic beats gentle and avoid gender-stereotyped conflict that invites argument rather than warmth.

title: Interest and investment in fictional romances.
venue: Psychology of Aesthetics Creativity and the Arts
finding: The OpenAlex record carries no usable abstract (only a note on supplementary/corrected material); keywords are 'romance fiction' and 'reader engagement'. Content not verified from the record.
why_for_us: Potentially central (who invests in fictional romances) but must be read in full before use; treat as a lead, not as evidence.

title: Parasocial Romantic Relationships: Falling in Love with Media Figures
finding: Monograph by Tukachinsky Forster (book with descriptive abstract): argues that parasocial romantic relationships - one-sided romantic feelings toward media figures, from adolescent celebrity crushes to anime fans who 'marry' characters - are profound and pervasive.
why_for_us: Background reference for why viewers form feelings toward on-screen couples; the micro-drama should invite liking the pair, not invite a viewer crush on one actor.

title: Parasocial romantic relationships, romantic beliefs, and relationship outcomes in USA adolescents: rehearsing love or setting oneself up to fail?
finding: Two surveys (153 adolescents aged 13-17; 274 college students 18-22, retrospective): emotional involvement in a parasocial romance was related to more idealised romantic beliefs in both samples; in college students, stronger adolescent emotional involvement went with lower relationship satisfaction and less favourable views of the current partner; physical attraction to the figure showed no such associations.
why_for_us: Effects are documented mainly for adolescents; with a 40-65 professional audience the risk of shaping beliefs is low, but the pair should still model a realistic, respectful relationship.

title: Romantic Parasocial Attachments and the Development of Romantic Scripts, Schemas and Beliefs among Adolescents
finding: Survey of college women (recall design; n not in abstract): more intense recalled adolescent romantic parasocial attachments were associated with higher relationship-contingent self-esteem, more negative evaluations of sexual experience and greater likelihood of passionate love.
why_for_us: Confirms romantic attachment to characters is common in youth; our older audience is more likely to watch the pair from a 'supporter' distance, so write for warmth and rooting, not for viewer infatuation.

title: Parasocial Romance: A Social Exchange Perspective
venue: Interpersona An International Journal on Personal Relationships
finding: Survey (n not in abstract) of perceived costs and benefits of real-life and parasocial romances: stronger parasocial romances went with greater perceived benefits relative to costs, and these benefits resembled those of real-life relationships, with some unique costs.
why_for_us: Viewers seek the same rewards from fictional romance as from real ones (warmth, companionship); short episodes can deliver small, regular 'rewards' (a glance, a shared joke) to keep viewers returning.

title: Dancing on My Own: Parasocial Love, Romantic Loneliness, and Imagined Interaction
finding: Survey of 224 Chinese college students: romantic loneliness was negatively related to parasocial love only in males, not females; imagined interaction with the persona (frequency, valence, compensation, relationship maintenance) was positively related to parasocial love.
why_for_us: Male viewers do engage romantically with characters, but differently; do not assume a romance thread works only for women in the notary audience.

title: Intimacy despite distance: The dark triad and romantic parasocial interactions
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
finding: Between-subjects experiment with 116 young adults in Germany: high dark-triad scorers engaged more in emotional love and responses to the character but not physical love; Machiavellian and psychopathic viewers tended to perceive the narrative as 'corny', which reduced engagement; interacting with the character raised relatedness gratification regardless of the romantic connotation.
why_for_us: The 'corny' reaction is a real risk with sceptical, analytical viewers; understate the romance and keep relatedness (team, mentor, shared work) as the main source of warmth.

title: Fictosexuality, Fictoromance, and Fictophilia: A Qualitative Study of Love and Desire for Fictional Characters
finding: Qualitative thematic analysis of 71 online discussions: five themes - fictophilic paradox, stigma, behaviours, asexuality and 'supernormal stimuli' - describe lasting love or desire for fictional characters.
why_for_us: Extreme form of character attachment; marginal for our audience, cited only to mark the far end of the spectrum.

title: Falling for fictional men: the social surrogacy of book boyfriends
finding: Survey of 494 readers recruited at book fairs and elsewhere: lower satisfaction with one's romantic relationship and higher psychological distress were related to stronger parasocial relationships with fictional characters, mainly as friends and emotional support; readers with such relationships scored higher on neuroticism and openness.
why_for_us: Fictional relationships serve emotional support more than romantic substitution; a warm, supportive dynamic between the apprentices (and their mentor) may resonate more than passion.

title: Older Adults’ Parasocial Relationships with Favorite Television Characters and Depressive Symptoms
finding: Survey of older adults (n not in abstract), SOC model: parasocial relationships with favourite TV characters often provide companionship; three-way interactions showed, e.g., stronger parasocial relationships predicted more depressive symptoms for anxious older adults in low-quality parent-child relationships.
why_for_us: Older viewers do bond with recurring TV characters; recurring faces across episodes (Kuba, Zosia, the senior notary) are an asset for a 40-65 audience.

title: Exploring the Paradox of the Enjoyment of Sad Films
finding: Three studies developing the Sad-Film Scale: sad reactions were positively related to enjoyment; females reported stronger enjoyment and sadness than males; the scale correlated with empathy, femininity and positive appraisals of sad emotions and predicted enjoyment of a specific sad film.
why_for_us: Being moved is itself rewarding; a small bittersweet beat (e.g., Zosia nearly leaving the office) can raise enjoyment, especially among empathic viewers.

title: An Examination of Factors Related to Sex Differences In Enjoyment of Sad Films
finding: Three studies (Beaches vs Brian's Song; film descriptions): females and communal (feminine) viewers reported greater enjoyment of sad films, particularly those featuring relational themes; gender-role identity and film theme mattered, not only biological sex.
why_for_us: Relational themes appeal to communal viewers of any sex; frame the romance as care and teamwork (communal) to reach both men and women in notary offices.

title: Tears or Fears? Comparing Gender Stereotypes about Movie Preferences to Actual Preferences
finding: Two studies on 17 genres: gender stereotypes existed for 15 genres and actual gender differences for 11; stereotypes were mostly accurate in direction but overestimated the size of differences for 10 of 17 genres.
why_for_us: Men's dislike of romance is smaller than assumed; a light romance thread need not alienate male notaries.

title: Age Differences in Adults' Emotional Motivations for Exposure to Films
finding: Questionnaire with younger (18-25, N=188), middle (26-49, N=92) and older adults (50+, N=93): younger adults most wanted negative emotions, dark or violent content and escape; older adults were most interested in emotional stability and uplifting, heartwarming content.
why_for_us: For a 40-65 audience, a heartwarming couple subplot fits better than dark, angsty romance; keep the thriller tension in the case, warmth in the couple.

title: When meaning matters more: Media preferences across the adult life span.
finding: Two studies with US (and German) adults aged 18-86 rating programme descriptions and trailers: anticipated meaningfulness predicted viewing interest more strongly for older than younger adults; warmth (but not funniness) was more predictive of meaningfulness for older adults.
why_for_us: Warmth that feels meaningful (helping a client, protecting a family's home) drives interest among older viewers; tie the romantic moments to meaningful work.

title: Age Differences in Nonhedonic Entertainment Experiences
finding: Experiment: younger adults 18-28 (n=84) vs older adults 62-87 (n=65) watched a sad or happy version of a meaningful film; older viewers reported higher eudaimonic entertainment, which among them was associated with positive affect and mixed emotions.
why_for_us: Older viewers appreciate meaningful, mixed-emotion moments; a short touching scene can work better than a comic flirt for senior notaries.

title: As Time Goes By: What Changes and What Remains the Same in Entertainment Experience Over the Life Span?
finding: Survey with film-scene ratings (n not in abstract): young adults sought emotionally intense experiences (thrill, tear-jerking) more than older adults, who preferred contemplative experiences; however, the same gratifications obtained predicted positive evaluations regardless of age.
why_for_us: Do not over-dramatise the romance for older viewers; quiet, contemplative beats are wanted, while gratifications that land still work across ages.

title: Reader and author gender and genre in Goodreads
venue: Journal of Librarianship and Information Science
finding: Quantitative analysis of reviews of 201,560 Goodreads books in the top 50 genres: strong gender differences in ratings within genres (e.g., female reviewers rated contemporary romance higher); relationships and romance were disproportionately mentioned by women even in mystery and fantasy.
why_for_us: Women value romance inside other genres (mystery!), which supports a romance thread inside a legal thriller for female staff; male viewers will rate on the case, so the case must carry the episode.

title: Who Feels All the Feels? Individual Differences in Emotional Responses to and Enjoyment of Depictions of Romantic Relationships
venue: Digital Commons - St. Norbert College (St. Norbert College)
finding: Experiment with 306 adults (comedy vs drama relationship portrayals): higher relationship satisfaction went with more hope in response to romantic movies and greater enjoyment; higher attachment avoidance went with less romantic feeling, hope and enjoyment; attachment anxiety increased enjoyment.
why_for_us: Romance pleases some viewers and leaves avoidant ones cold; keep each episode's main payoff in the legal plot so that no viewer is lost when the couple beat does not appeal.

title: The Feel-Good Film: Genre Features and Emotional Rewards
finding: Audience-perspective study (sample not in abstract): romantic comedy with a substantial share of drama is the most prototypical feel-good blend; fairy-tale likeness and lightness are key, yet trajectories include serious conflicts and are deeply moving; preferences differ greatly by gender and age.
why_for_us: A light romcom-plus-drama tone is the classic feel-good mix; combine a light couple thread with a serious legal stake.

title: Romance Dramas Viewership and It's Impact on Audiences' Romantic Ideals
finding: Narrative analysis of 50 Chinese romance dramas plus a survey of 655 viewers (in Chinese): gentle, understanding handsome men and independent, smart women were the favourite leads; about 30% of romance-drama viewers were men, who liked watching and discussing with partners; about two-thirds held positive marriage and love views.
why_for_us: A competent, self-reliant Zosia and a considerate Kuba match audience-preferred lead types; male viewers are a substantial minority of romance audiences.

title: Competition, Contracts, and Creativity: Evidence from Novel Writing in a Platform Market
finding: Natural experiment on a Chinese serial-novel platform: a regulation induced a massive entry of romance-genre novels; intensified competition made authors publish faster with weak effects on novelty, stronger for revenue-sharing books and early life-cycle stages.
why_for_us: Serialised romance is a crowded, mass genre on platforms; a notary micro-drama cannot compete on romance alone and should differentiate through its legal-world novelty.

title: Touring the land of romance: transnational Korean television drama consumption from online desires to offline intimacy
venue: Journal of Tourism and Cultural Change
finding: Digital archival research of fan forums plus ethnographic interviews with Hallyu tourists: the author argues that fans' romantic and intimate desires for Korean men are central to the transnational popularity of K-dramas and to Hallyu tourism.
why_for_us: Romance is a proven driver of global serial engagement, but the mechanism is desire for the male lead; for our audience aim for liking the pair, not idolising one actor.

title: 중국인들이 선호하는 한국 드라마의 특성 -인터넷 게시판에 나타난 시청의견을 중심으로-
venue: The Journal of the Korea Contents Association
finding: Analysis of Chinese internet-board viewer opinions on Korean dramas (Korean abstract): recent miniseries were preferred, and - unlike earlier studies - comic dramas were preferred over romance by theme; acting and story mattered more than Hallyu-star casting.
why_for_us: Contradicts 'romance sells': story quality and humour can matter more than the romance itself; keep the couple thread light and funny.

title: From Web Dramas to OTT Originals
finding: Book chapter (industry analysis, essay): Korean linear television relied on star talent and heteronormative romance narratives to secure audience ratings and international sales; web dramas and OTT platforms later made niche romance formats industrially viable.
why_for_us: Industry treats romance as a ratings tool; the short web format also allows niche framing (a romance among notarial apprentices) for a narrow professional audience.

title: An Analysis on the Relationship between Narrative Structure of TV Drama and Audience Ratings
venue: journal of the moving image technology associon of korea
finding: Single-case narrative analysis (no statistics in abstract) of the medical drama Romantic Dr. Kim Sabu: the author argues that its use of discontinuity, segmentation and cliffhangers between episodes corresponds with the trend of its audience ratings.
why_for_us: A professional (medical) drama can hold ratings through episode-end hooks; in 60-90 s episodes the end hook should come from the case, with a romantic glance as a secondary hook.

title: ‘They’re so predictable … but, I love them’: Analysing the appeal of Hallmark Christmas movies
finding: Q-methodology study of self-identified fans at Christmas Con 2019 (n not in abstract); per authors Hallmark's 41 new Christmas movies drew 85 million viewers in 2021; three fan types emerged: season celebrators, escapists, and viewers seeking a wholesome story with a happy ending.
why_for_us: Predictable, wholesome romance with a happy ending has a large loyal adult audience; predictability is not a defect if the tone is warm.

title: Unlikely Heroines? 'Women of a Certain Age' and Romantic Comedy
finding: Essay: romcom's critical standing is inversely related to its box-office pull (citing a survey where 2003-2008 romcoms averaged 46% with critics while two titles made $239m); Hollywood long excluded older women, though a sub-genre centring romance on older women has gained momentum.
why_for_us: Romance draws audiences despite critics; and older viewers are under-served - a mature secondary couple (e.g., senior notary) could speak to a 40-65 audience.

title: Does Television Viewing Cultivate Unrealistic Expectations About Marriage?
finding: Survey of 285 never-married university students: overall TV viewing was negatively associated with idealistic marriage expectations, but viewing of romantic genre programming (romantic comedies, soap operas) was positively associated with them, and these expectations were strongly related to marital intentions.
why_for_us: Genre-specific romance shapes expectations, but effects are shown in young singles; low risk for our audience, though avoid fairy-tale 'instant soulmate' framing.

title: Isn’t it romantic? Differential associations between romantic screen media genres and romantic beliefs.
finding: Survey of 625 college students on exposure to three romantic screen-media genres (abstract truncated in OpenAlex): investigates associations between genre exposure and idealistic romantic beliefs; detailed results not available in the record.
why_for_us: Supports genre-specific thinking about effects; results must be read in full before citing specifics.

title: I Did It Because I Never Stopped Loving You: The Effects of Media Portrayals of Persistent Pursuit on Beliefs About Stalking
finding: Experiment: a film depicting persistent pursuit as scary led to fewer stalking-supportive beliefs; a film depicting it as romantic increased stalking-supportive beliefs only among viewers high in perceived realism or transportation.
why_for_us: Never write Kuba's interest as persistent pursuit after a 'no' (waiting outside, repeated messages); in a workplace setting this also reads as harassment to a legal audience.

title: True love lasts forever: the influence of a popular teenage movie on Belgian girls’ romantic beliefs
finding: Experiment with 88 girls aged 11-14 (High School Musical): girls high in parasocial interaction endorsed more idealistic romantic beliefs after viewing; the effect decreased with increasing age.
why_for_us: Belief effects shrink with age, so the main risk for adult notaries is not belief change but credibility and taste.

title: Television and Movie Viewing Predict Adults’ Romantic Ideals and Relationship Satisfaction
finding: Survey of 306 adults aged 18-64 in relationships: viewing each genre (relationship reality TV, TV drama, comedy, soap opera, romantic movies) was positively associated with romantic ideals; TV drama and romantic movies were the strongest predictors of 'love conquers all' and relationship satisfaction; genres related positively to satisfaction via romantic ideals; no moderation by age.
why_for_us: For adults the association of romantic viewing with satisfaction is positive, not harmful; a hopeful, kind romance is acceptable for a mixed-age audience.

title: Is Seeing Believing? Hallmark Movie Viewership and Relationship Beliefs
finding: Nationwide survey of 279 heterosexual married adults: more frequent Hallmark movie viewing was associated with more unrealistic relationship beliefs, destiny beliefs, and the belief that opposite-sex friendships are problematic, beyond attachment, relationship length and total TV use.
why_for_us: Idealised romance may cue the idea that male-female colleagues cannot just be friends; show Kuba and Zosia's professional respect first, and avoid jealousy plots involving other colleagues.

title: “Frankly, My Dear, I Just Might Give a damn:” An Experiment Investigating Preexisting Beliefs and Reasons to Watch Romantic Comedies on Reports of Beliefs, Mood, and Enjoyment
finding: Pretest-posttest experiment with 358 undergraduates: prior romantic beliefs predicted reduced beliefs after a 'challenge' film and greater enjoyment after an 'ideal' film; motives for watching also mattered.
why_for_us: Viewers enjoy romance that confirms what they already believe; a gentle, conventional slow-burn suits a conservative professional audience better than a subversive take.

title: Discrete Emotions Shape Gender Role Attitudes: Exploring the Impact of Gender-Stereotyped Douyin Urban Romantic Short Dramas on Chinese Youth
finding: Pretest-posttest control-group experiment with 320 Chinese students (160 m, 160 f) on gender-stereotyped Douyin romance short dramas: male stereotypes evoked joy and sadness and strengthened traditional male-role identification; female stereotypes triggered disgust and fear and promoted acceptance of traditional female roles; young males were more easily assimilated.
why_for_us: Vertical romance shorts with stereotyped roles can polarise reactions by gender; avoid the 'domineering CEO / helpless girl' template common in short dramas.

title: The Motives for and Consequences of Viewing Television Medical Dramas
finding: Uses-and-gratifications survey of college students (n not in abstract): the primary motive for watching medical dramas was not health information; entertainment motives indirectly predicted use of health information via involvement with the dramas.
why_for_us: People watch profession dramas for entertainment (incl. characters' relationships), and involvement then carries the informational content; the romance can raise involvement that carries the SaaS message.

title: Hospital doctors' Opinions regarding educational Utility, public Sentiment and career Effects of Medical television Dramas: the HOUSE MD study
finding: Questionnaire of hospital doctors in Wales (200 of 372 returned, 54%): 65% watched medical dramas more than once, 69% for entertainment and 8% for education; 82% found them unrepresentative of daily practice and 10% realistic; junior doctors watched more and more often identified with fictional doctors.
why_for_us: Professionals watch dramas about their own job for fun yet judge them unrealistic; notaries will forgive romance but not procedural errors - have every notarial detail checked by a notary.

title: TV medical dramas: health sciences students’ viewing habits and potential for teaching issues related to bioethics and professionalism
finding: Questionnaire of 355 health-science students: 93.5% watched TV series and 49.6% watched medical dramas more than once a week; most-remembered topics were medical errors, inappropriate professional behaviour and death; most considered professionalism depicted positively.
why_for_us: Future professionals binge dramas about their field and remember misconduct most; a romance that breaches professional rules (e.g., favouritism in a deed) would be the memorable part - avoid it.

title: Bioethics and professionalism in popular television medical dramas
finding: Systematic content analysis of one season each of Grey's Anatomy and House M.D.: the programmes were rife with bioethical issues and egregious deviations from professionalism norms, with exemplary professionalism shown much less often.
why_for_us: Popular workplace dramas buy drama with unprofessional conduct; for a brand aimed at notaries the couple must stay professionally impeccable on the job.

title: Perceived Realism of Television Medical Dramas and Perceptions About Physicians
venue: Journal of Media Psychology Theories Methods and Applications
finding: Survey of college students on ER, Grey's Anatomy and House: of three realism dimensions (plausibility, typicality, narrative consistency), narrative consistency predicted positive perceptions of physicians.
why_for_us: Internal consistency of characters matters more than documentary realism; keep Kuba's and Zosia's behaviour consistent across episodes.

title: Different Positive Feelings Leading to Different Ad Evaluations: The Case of Coziness, Excitement, and Romance
finding: Experiment (sample not stated in abstract): ad- and context-evoked coziness, excitement and romance had different effects on ad evaluations; romantic (and cozy, exciting) ads scored best in a feeling-congruent context.
why_for_us: A romantic beat works best when the surrounding context is congruent; do not cut from a tender moment straight to a hard product pitch - bridge with tone.

title: The effect of exposure to sexual appeals in advertisements on memory, attitude, and purchase intention: a meta-analytic review
finding: Meta-analysis of experiments: sexual appeals improved ad recognition/recall (d=.38) but not brand recall (d=.09, n.s.); no effect on ad attitude overall (d=-.07), with men more positive (d=.27) and women negative (d=-.38); small negative effect on brand attitude (d=-.22); no effect on purchase intention (d=.01).
why_for_us: Sexualised content would hurt the brand with female staff and not help recall of the SaaS; keep the romance chaste and use it for attention to the story, not as the selling device.

title: Ethical Judgments of Sexual Appeals in Print Advertising
finding: Study of consumer responses (ethics scale, ad and brand attitude, purchase intention; n not in abstract): a strong overt sexual appeal in a print ad was not well received regardless of respondent gender.
why_for_us: Overt sexuality is judged unethical by both sexes; a professional notary audience is the least likely to tolerate it.

title: Same-Sex Couples in Advertisements: An Investigation of the Role of Implicit Attitudes on Cognitive Processing and Evaluation
finding: Three studies (physiology during 10 TV ads; replications in non-student samples): participants responded less positively to ads featuring same-sex couples than other-sex couples, and negative implicit attitudes toward homosexuality predicted more negative affect, less attention and less liking.
why_for_us: Couple depictions in ads are processed through viewers' implicit attitudes; for any couple, test the episode with real notary-office staff before publishing.

title: Interracial Couples in Ads: Do Consumers' Gender and Racial Differences Affect Their Reactions?
venue: Journal of Current Issues & Research in Advertising
finding: Experiment (n not in abstract): ads depicting black-white couples elicited more negative emotions and less favourable ad and brand attitudes than same-race couple ads; reactions were unrelated to respondents' own race and gender.
why_for_us: Couple casting in ads carries audience-attitude effects on the brand; pre-test the pair with the target audience.

title: Brand romance: a complementary approach to explain emotional attachment toward brands
finding: Four studies (student samples) developing a 12-item, three-factor brand-romance scale: brand romance explained loyalty significantly better than attitudes; authors advise continuous novelty to keep attraction to a brand strong.
why_for_us: Metaphor for the SaaS itself: keep the brand 'romance' alive with novelty; for B2B software loyalty, the series should introduce new features as new 'chapters'.
